priya.name: Dr. Priya Nair
priya.role: materials scientist (someone who studies what things are made of and how they behave)

case.title: Next Year’s Trophy
case.hook: Dr. Priya Nair here. You found the real trophy! Now Mr. Ortiz wants a NEW one for next year. The engraver, R. Vega, sent four designs. Only one fits every need.

order.head: PALMETTO SPRINGS DUCK DERBY
order.title: Trophy order form · for next year
rows: A trophy for the winning duck’s owner
It sits outside by the pond, so it must survive rain
It must not break if a little kid drops it
A 5-year-old must lift it: under 500 grams in all
order.designsLabel: R. Vega’s four designs (add up each one!)

case.question: Which design should R. Vega build for next year’s trophy?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: Taking something apart does not change its mass. The robot’s parts added up to 60 g, the same as the whole. So add up a design’s parts to find its total.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: sticker every property
clues.t: One material can belong to many groups. Foil bends AND keeps water out. Look for the material with every property the job needs.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: the job test rigs
clues.t: The job decides. Steel held up the bridge but failed the umbrella, the sponge and the pan handle. Heavy and strong is not always best.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: the drip and bend lab
clues.t: A classification table shows which materials pass EVERY test at once. Only plastic wrap and foil kept water out AND bent.

solve.title: Which design fits every need?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Design A, all brass. Heavy and strong must be best.
options.why: Check Clues 1 and 3. Add up Design A: 606 grams. That is over the 500-gram limit, and heavy is not the same as best.

options.t: Design B, glass and wood. The shiniest, at 410 grams.
options.why: Check Clue 3. The order says it must not break if a little kid drops it. Glass shatters.

options.t: Design C, aluminum and plastic. Rain can’t soak in, it won’t shatter, and it adds up to 254 grams.
options.why: Case cracked! Design C passes all three needs at once, just like a winner in your classification table.

options.t: Design D, cardboard. The lightest: only 110 grams.
options.why: Check Clues 2 and 4. Cardboard soaks up water. One rainy derby and the trophy turns to mush.

takeapart.title: Take it apart

why.t: A pile of pieces LOOKS smaller. Does it really have less mass?

todo: Drag each part onto Scale 2, or tap the part and then the scales.
Watch the scales and the adding tape.
takeapart.alt: Two model kitchen scales. A toy robot made of colored blocks stands on Scale 1. Scale 2 is empty.
takeapart.model: A model test. Try it at home with snap-together blocks and a kitchen scale.
takeapart.predictQ: The whole robot weighs 60 grams. The pile of parts will weigh…

results.same: You called it! The pile weighs exactly 60 g, the same as the whole robot.
results.more: Surprise! The pile weighs exactly 60 g, the same as the whole robot. Spreading out added nothing.
results.less: Surprise! The pile weighs exactly 60 g, the same as the whole robot. Nothing got lost.

takeapart.q: Why does the pile weigh the same as the whole robot?

opts.t: Taking it apart did not add or remove any matter. The whole equals the sum of its parts.

opts.miss: Check the tape: 8 + 20 + 6 + 6 + 10 + 10. Add it up yourself.
Look at Scale 2. Spread out, the pieces still added up to 60 g.

takeapart.win: The whole equals the sum of its parts. Nothing was lost! Clue 1!

stickers.title: Sticker every true property

why.t: Each sticker is a group. A material can wear many stickers.

todo: Drag a sticker onto a material, or tap the sticker and then the material.
Each card shows how many stickers fit it. Fill every spot.
A wrong sticker bounces off. Read why.
stickers.sheetLabel: Your sticker sheet (stickers never run out)

miss.stiff: Stretch a rubber band. It bends and stretches easily.
miss.soak: Water rolls right off rubber. It can’t soak in.
miss.magnet: Rubber has no iron in it. A magnet won’t grab it.

miss.stiff: Crumple foil in your hand. It bends easily.
miss.soak: Water beads up on foil. It can’t soak in.
miss.magnet: Foil is a metal, but aluminum does NOT stick to a magnet. Try it on your fridge!

miss.bends: Try to bend a block of wood. It stays stiff.
miss.water: Bare wood soaks up water slowly. That’s why decks get painted.
miss.magnet: Wood has no iron in it. A magnet slides right off.

miss.bends: Glass can’t bend. It breaks first!
miss.soak: Water can’t soak into glass. That’s why we drink from it.
miss.magnet: Glass has no iron in it. A magnet won’t stick.

miss.stiff: Hold up a sheet of paper. It flops over: it bends.
miss.water: Spill on paper and it gets soggy. Water soaks in.
miss.magnet: Paper has no iron in it. A magnet won’t grab it.

miss.stiff: Plastic wrap is floppy. It bends.
miss.soak: Water slides off plastic wrap. That’s why it keeps food fresh.
miss.magnet: Plastic has no iron in it. A magnet won’t stick.

miss.bends: Try to bend a nail with your fingers. It stays stiff.
miss.soak: Water can’t soak into iron. (It can rust on the outside, though!)

miss.stiff: A cotton shirt folds and drapes. It bends.
miss.water: Spill on a cotton shirt and it gets wet through. It soaks water up.
miss.magnet: Cotton has no iron in it. A magnet won’t grab it.

stickers.countWord: materials wearing every sticker that fits
stickers.mostLine: {names} wore the most stickers: {n}. Every material wore at least two. One material, many groups!
stickers.q: The rubber band wore BOTH Bends and Waterproof. What does that tell you?

opts.t: One material can belong to more than one group. Which group matters depends on the job.
Rubber should only be in one group.
opts.miss: Look at the rubber band card. Both stickers stuck, because both are true.
Look at the plastic wrap and the foil. Both bend AND keep water out.

stickers.win: One material, many groups. Sort by the property the job needs. Clue 2!

rigs.title: The job test rigs

why.t: A setup that makes a material do the job: rain on an umbrella, a truck on a bridge.

todo: Pick a job tab. Read what it needs.
Drag a material into the rig (or tap it, then the rig). Press Run the test.
If it fails, swap. Pass all four jobs, then try steel in every rig.

lines.plastic: Plastic bends to fold up, and the rain rolls right off.
lines.paper: Rain soaked right through the paper, and it sagged and tore.
lines.foam: Foam soaks up rain like a sponge. Soggy and heavy!
lines.steel: Waterproof, yes. But steel is too stiff to fold and too heavy to hold up. Heavier is not better.
lines.wood: Wood can’t fold up, and bare wood soaks up rain.

jobs.needs: soaks up water + squishes into corners

lines.foam: Foam is full of tiny holes that soak up the spill, and it squishes back into shape.
lines.paper: Paper soaks up a little, then falls apart when you scrub.
lines.plastic: Water slides right off plastic. The spill stays put.
lines.steel: Steel can’t soak up a single drop. The spill stays.
lines.wood: Wood is too stiff to squish into corners, and it soaks up water very slowly.

jobs.needs: stays stiff + strong enough for a truck

lines.steel: Steel stays stiff and strong under the heavy truck.
lines.wood: A thick wooden beam is stiff and strong too. Lots of small bridges are made of wood.
lines.foam: Foam squished and sagged as soon as the truck rolled on.
lines.paper: Paper folded right under the truck.
lines.plastic: This thin plastic bent and sagged under the load.

jobs.needs: stays cool enough to hold + stiff

lines.wood: Wood carries heat slowly, so the handle stays cool enough to hold.
lines.plastic: Heat-proof plastic carries heat slowly too, so the handle stays cool enough to hold.
lines.steel: Steel carries heat fast. The handle got too hot to hold. Strong is not the same as right!
lines.foam: Foam is soft and floppy, and it melts near a hot stove.
lines.paper: Paper is floppy, and it could catch fire next to a stove.

rigs.mustLine: All four jobs passed! One more test: put {m} in every rig. Can the strongest material win them all? Still to try: {jobs}.
rigs.dropLine: Put a material in the rig
rigs.q: Steel held up the bridge, but it failed the other three jobs. What does that prove?

opts.t: There is no one best material. The job decides which properties matter.
Steel is still the best material.
opts.miss: Check your tests. Steel failed the umbrella, the sponge and the pan handle.
Steel is the heaviest material here, and it lost three jobs. Heavy is not the same as right.

rigs.win: Four jobs, four winners. The JOB decides the material. Clue 3!

tally.afterText: Now try it with the real trophy:
tally.title: The 412-gram puzzle

why.q: Why is the trophy in pieces?
why.t: R. Vega took the real trophy apart to engrave it. Mr. Ortiz is worried: the pile LOOKS smaller. Is brass missing?

todo: Tap each part on the bench.
Compare the total with the whole trophy: 412 grams.
tally.emptyLine: Tap a part to print it.
tally.matchLine: The parts add up to {x} g: exactly what the whole trophy weighed. Nothing went missing!
tally.q: Mr. Ortiz thought some brass was missing because the pile looked smaller. What do you tell him?

opts.t: Nothing is missing. The parts add up to 412 g, the mass of the whole trophy.
Some brass got lost when it came apart.
opts.miss: Check the tape. Every gram is there: 412.

opts.t: A pile always weighs less than the whole.
opts.miss: The robot pile in the Warm-Up weighed the same as the whole robot. So does this one.

tally.done: Wow! The whole equals the sum of its parts, for a toy robot AND a real brass trophy.

why.t: A chart with a row for each material and a column for each test.

todo: Press Drip water, watch, and tap what you saw. Then Bend it.
Test all five. Then read your table.
driplab.model: A model lab table. Try it at home with a spoon of water.

water.q: What did the water do on the {m}?

opts.t: It beaded up and sat on top

bend.q: What did the {m} do when you bent it?

driplab.wrongSaw: Look again at the swatch. What did it really do?
driplab.doneLine: Your table is full. Read it like a scientist.
driplab.q: Read your table. Which two materials kept water out AND bent?

opts.miss: Check the Water test column. Those two soaked the water up.
Check the Bend test column for cardboard.

driplab.win: Your table sorted the evidence: only two materials pass BOTH tests. That’s how you pick a raincoat. Clue 4!

sunnote.title: The late note

note.t: One more thing! The awards are at noon in July, out in the sun, and the winner holds the trophy up by its handles. Is Design C still okay?

sunnote.pickQ: A new need: the handles must stay cool enough to hold in the hot sun. Which handles now?

handles.why: In the July noon sun, metal handles soak up heat and carry it straight to your fingers. Ouch!
Wood carries heat slowly, so it stays cool enough to hold. The paint keeps rain out.
Hard plastic carries heat slowly too, and rain can’t soak in.
Glass handles would snap off if a little kid dropped the trophy. Need 2!

sunnote.totalQ: Add up the parts. What is the new total?
sunnote.win: New total: {x} g. Still under 500 g, cool to hold, and it survives rain and drops. A new need changed the pick!

q1.A: Classifying doesn’t change the materials. What did the stickers do?
q1.C: Paint changes how a thing looks. Classifying puts things into groups.

q2.B: Absorbent means it soaks up water. What happened to the paper umbrella in the rain rig?
q2.C: Heavy and stiff can’t fold up. Remember the steel umbrella?

q3.A: Check the rigs: steel failed three jobs.
q3.B: Plastic failed the sponge rig. No ONE material wins every job.

photos.title: Picked for the hottest job
todo: Tap each number on the photo.
Then match each material to its job.

why.t: A real photo from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida: a worker lifts a space shuttle heat tile out of a 2,200-degree oven.

photos.alt: A worker in a shiny silver suit, thick gloves and a gold face shield holds a white holder with a glowing red-hot heat tile on it.
photos.license: public domain, via NASA Image Library

hotspots.label: The glowing tile
hotspots.t: A shuttle heat tile, fresh from a 2,200-degree oven. It glows red-hot, but it is full of tiny air pockets, so heat crawls through it very slowly. Tiles like it covered the space shuttle to block the heat of coming home from space.

hotspots.label: Thick gloves
hotspots.t: Thick, puffy gloves carry heat slowly, so the worker’s hands stay safe. Same idea as a wooden pan handle!

hotspots.label: The silver suit
hotspots.t: The suit is coated with shiny metal. It reflects (bounces back) the heat glowing off the oven and the tile.

hotspots.label: The gold face shield
hotspots.t: A thin gold-colored coating reflects heat and bright glare, but the worker can still see through it.

task.q: Match it: which label shows the material picked for each job?

items.evid: A shuttle heat tile survives a 2,200-degree oven. It was picked for one job: blocking heat.
items.miss: Look for the thing that is glowing.

items.step: Keep hands safe by carrying heat slowly
items.evid: Thick gloves carry heat slowly, like a wooden pan handle.
items.miss: What is the worker holding things with?

items.step: Bounce heat away from the body
items.evid: A shiny metal-coated suit reflects heat away from the worker’s body.
items.miss: Look for the big shiny thing the worker is wearing.

items.step: Block glare but still let you see
items.evid: A gold-coated face shield blocks heat and glare, but you can see through it.

task.win: Four materials, four jobs, one very hot room. Every one was picked for its properties, just like your trophy.

part1.label: Part 1 · sticker every property (Clue 2)
part1.script: Each sticker is a group. Drag Bends onto the rubber band. Does Waterproof fit too? Every card shows how many stickers it needs. A wrong sticker bounces off, so read why. The iron nail might surprise you.

part2.label: Part 2 · the job test rigs (Clue 3)
part2.script: Engineers test before they build. Pick a job tab and read what it needs. Drag a material into the rig, then press Run the test. If it fails, swap and run again. Can steel win every job?

explore.script: Five swatches, two tests. Press Drip water and watch: does it bead up, or soak in? Then press Bend it. Tap what you saw. Your classification table fills in row by row. Read it at the end.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this tell how to sort materials, or how to pick one for a job?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: Engineers choose the material whose properties match the job, so no one material is best for everything.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “properties”, “job” and “material”. Those words hold the big idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
